title: PAUL DIDN’T CELEBRATE THEIR SEXUAL TOLERANCE—HE REBUKED IT
paragraphs: PAUL DIDN’T CELEBRATE THEIR SEXUAL TOLERANCE—HE REBUKED IT
Corinth called it something to tolerate. Paul called the church to mourn, confront sin, and remember what the blood of Jesus had washed them from.
There is a kind of Christianity that desperately wants Jesus as Savior but becomes uncomfortable the moment He starts speaking as Lord.
It wants grace without repentance.
Love without truth.
Forgiveness without transformation.
A cross that comforts us, but never contradicts us.
And if the apostle Paul walked into some Christian conversations today, one of the first accusations thrown at him might be that he was being too judgmental.
Because when the Corinthian church became strangely comfortable with sexual sin inside its own fellowship, Paul did not congratulate them for being tolerant.
He was horrified.
Not because sexual sinners were beyond grace.
Paul knew better than almost anyone that scandalous people could be redeemed.
Not because Christians were supposed to despise unbelievers.
Paul explicitly corrected that misunderstanding.
And not because sexual sin was the only sin that mattered.
In the very same passages, Paul confronted greed, idolatry, drunkenness, slander, theft, and other forms of unrighteousness.
What disturbed Paul was something more revealing.
A church bearing the name of Jesus had begun boasting when it should have been grieving.
That should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because Corinth is not merely an ancient city we can examine from a safe historical distance.
Sometimes Corinth is sitting in our pew.
Sometimes Corinth is scrolling on our phone.
Sometimes Corinth is hidden in our browser history.
Sometimes Corinth is the relationship we keep defending.
Sometimes Corinth is the secret compromise we renamed so we would no longer have to repent of it.
Sometimes Corinth is us.

Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 5 about a case of sexual immorality within the congregation so serious that he says it was not even ordinarily tolerated among the surrounding Gentiles: a man had his father’s wife.
Then comes the sentence that exposes the spiritual condition of the church.
Paul says, in Greek:
Καὶ ὑμεῖς πεφυσιωμένοι ἐστέ
Kaì hymeîs pephysiōménoi esté.
“And you are arrogant!”
The verb behind that accusation comes from φυσιόω — physioō, carrying the idea of being puffed up, inflated, made proud.
The scandal was terrible.
But Paul was also alarmed by the church’s attitude toward the scandal.
They were puffed up.
He immediately tells them that they should rather have mourned.
Think about that.
Paul did not ask, “How can we make sin feel safer?”
He essentially asked, “Why aren’t you grieving?”
That distinction matters.
Because biblical love does not rejoice when somebody is destroying himself.
Biblical love does not require hatred of a sinner.
It requires hatred of what enslaves the sinner.
There is an enormous difference.
A doctor does not prove compassion by looking at cancer and saying, “Who am I to judge?”
A firefighter does not demonstrate kindness by watching a house burn because warning the family might make them uncomfortable.
And Christians do not love people by pretending that something God calls sin becomes holy merely because our culture has learned to celebrate it.
But before Christians point this passage outward, Paul forces the finger back toward the church.
That is where this becomes painful.
Paul specifically explains that he is not demanding complete separation from sexually immoral people in the world.
He says that doing so would practically require believers to leave the world altogether.
Then he writes:
τί γάρ μοι τοὺς ἔξω κρίνειν;
Ti gár moi toùs éxō krínein?
“For what have I to do with judging outsiders?”
And then:
οὐχὶ τοὺς ἔσω ὑμεῖς κρίνετε;
Ouchì toùs ésō hymeîs krínete?
“Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?”
That destroys two opposite distortions at once.
The first distortion says Christians must affirm whatever the surrounding culture approves.
Paul refuses that.
The second says Christians should spend their lives angrily policing unbelievers while ignoring corruption among professing Christians.
Paul refuses that too.
His immediate concern is the holiness of the church.
Not a self-righteous church.
Not a cruel church.
A holy church.
A church that understands that the name of Jesus is too precious to attach casually to deliberate, unrepentant rebellion against Jesus.
And here we have to be painfully careful.
Because church discipline has sometimes been twisted into humiliation, authoritarian control, selective outrage, gossip, and spiritual abuse.
That is not a faithful application of Paul.
Biblical correction is never permission for Christians to become cruel.

Jesus Himself taught that confrontation should seek restoration. Paul elsewhere tells believers that if someone is caught in transgression, those who are spiritual should restore that person “in a spirit of gentleness,” while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
The goal is not:
“Look how disgusting you are.”
The goal is:
“Come home.”
That changes everything.
Because the Gospel does not expose sin so spectators can throw stones.
The Gospel exposes sin so sinners can run to a Savior.
And then Paul takes Corinth deeper.

In 1 Corinthians 6 he gives a sobering catalogue of sinful patterns incompatible with inheriting the kingdom of God. Among the Greek terms in the passage are μαλακοί — malakoi and ἀρσενοκοῖται — arsenokoitai.
These words have generated substantial modern discussion, so they deserve more care than slogans allow.

Malakos literally has the basic sense of “soft,” but in certain ancient contexts could carry sexual connotations. Arsenokoitēs is a comparatively rare compound formed from arsēn, “male,” and koitē, “bed,” with sexual implications. Many scholars have also noted its apparent verbal relationship to the Greek wording of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 in the Septuagint.
Translations differ over how best to render these terms into modern English, and responsible interpretation should acknowledge those lexical questions rather than pretending they do not exist.
But neither should uncertainty over the most precise English gloss be turned into permission to erase Paul’s broader sexual ethic.
Paul’s understanding of sexual holiness is not built on one disputed English word.

Across his letters, sexual activity is treated as morally accountable before God, and in 1 Corinthians itself Paul positively directs sexual union toward marriage, speaking of husband and wife in 1 Corinthians 7.
Yet here is where some Christians stop reading too early.
They quote the warning.
They underline the sins.
They identify everyone they think belongs on the list.
And they miss one of the most breathtaking sentences in the entire chapter.
Paul looks at this church filled with redeemed people and says:
καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε
Kaì taûtá tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That one word can make a sinner cry.
You were.
Paul does not say there had never been sexually immoral people among them.
There had been.
He does not say there had never been idolaters.
There had been.
Adulterers.
Thieves.
Greedy people.
Drunkards.
Slanderers.
Swindlers.
People with histories.
People with scars.
People carrying memories they probably wished they could erase.
The church at Corinth was not a museum filled with people who had never fallen.
It was supposed to be a community of people whose identities were being rewritten by Jesus Christ.
And Paul continues:
ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε
allà apelousasthe.
“But you were washed.”
ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε
allà hēgiásthēte.
“But you were sanctified.”
ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε
allà edikaiṓthēte.
“But you were justified.”
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
Read that again slowly.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
This is why biblical Christianity can never be reduced to screaming at sexual sinners.
Because Christianity is fundamentally the announcement that sinners can be washed.
The adulterer can be washed.
The sexually broken can be washed.
The porn-addicted can be washed.
The greedy can be washed.
The drunkard can be washed.
The liar can be washed.
The self-righteous religious hypocrite can be washed.
The person whose sexual history fills them with shame can be washed.
The person who thought they had gone too far can be washed.
The person hiding behind church clothes and a worship smile while secretly losing a war nobody knows about can be washed.
And so can you.
Not by pretending your sin was never sin.
By bringing it to Jesus.
That is the scandal of grace.
Grace does not stand over the grave of your old life and tell you the corpse was beautiful.
Grace calls you out of the grave.
Jesus does not save us because our rebellion was harmless.
He saves us because His mercy is greater than our rebellion.
At the cross, holiness and mercy do not compete.
They meet.
Jesus never needed to redefine darkness to prove that He loved people trapped inside it.
He stepped into our darkness.
He carried sin.
He bore judgment.
He died.
And He rose again.
So when Christ calls you to repent, He is not trying to steal your life.
He is calling you out of death.
Maybe this is where the article stopped being about Corinth.
Maybe you came here thinking about somebody else.
A denomination.
A pastor.
A gay person.
A sexually immoral culture.
A compromised church.
A relative.
A celebrity.
“Those people.”
But what if the Holy Spirit has been quietly moving the mirror?
What are you defending that Jesus has been asking you to surrender?
What are you watching when nobody is there?
What relationship are you unwilling to place beneath the lordship of Christ?
What fantasy keeps returning?
What secret messages would terrify you if they became public?
What bitterness have you baptized as discernment?
What greed have you renamed ambition?
What drunkenness have you called coping?
What pride have you disguised as holiness?
What sin in somebody else makes you furious while your own favorite sin receives endless excuses?
Be careful.
The Pharisee can be sexually clean and still desperately need Jesus.
The prodigal can smell like the pigpen and still be running toward the Father.
Both need grace.
Both need repentance.
Both need Christ.
Paul's rebuke of Corinth therefore gives us no permission to hate sexually broken people.
It gives us no permission to mock them, harass them, dehumanize them, or treat them as uniquely unreachable.
Every human being bears dignity as one made in the image of God.
Every sinner should hear the Gospel.
Every repentant sinner who comes to Christ should discover that the church has room for redeemed people with ugly histories.
Because if ugly histories disqualified people from grace, Christianity would have no congregation.
We would all be outside.
The Christian message is not, “Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.”
It is, “Come to Jesus. He alone can save you, forgive you, cleanse you, and make you new.”
But coming to Jesus means coming to Jesus as Lord.
Not merely adviser.
Not accessory.
Not inspirational figure.
Lord.
This is where modern ears sometimes struggle with biblical grace.
We have been taught to imagine acceptance as the highest possible expression of love.
Jesus offers something infinitely greater.
Transformation.
He loves us too deeply to merely affirm the chains that keep us from Him.
Paul later says something astonishing about sexual sin:
οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν;
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?”
Then comes the foundation beneath Christian sexual ethics:
οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν
“You are not your own.”
And then:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς
“You were bought with a price.”
Therefore, Paul says, glorify God in your body.
There it is.
Christian holiness is not ultimately about winning culture wars.
It is about belonging to Christ.
You were bought with a price.
Blood was shed.
A cross was raised.
The Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
So your body matters.
Your sexuality matters.
Your private life matters.
Your repentance matters.
Your holiness matters.
Not because holiness purchases salvation.
Christ purchased salvation.
We pursue holiness because we belong to the One who purchased us.
And maybe you failed last night.
Maybe you promised God it would never happen again and then it happened again.
Maybe you are reading this after deleting evidence.
Maybe your marriage is wounded because of what you did.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe shame has been whispering that you should stay away from God until you become respectable again.
Do not believe that voice.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Bring darkness into the light.
If necessary, seek faithful pastoral accountability and qualified professional help.
Cut off access to what keeps dragging you backward.
End what must end.
Repair what can biblically be repaired.
Tell the truth.
Not because confession earns forgiveness.
Because Jesus already opened the door for repentant sinners to come into the light.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation does not mean no transformation.
Grace is not God shrugging at your chains.
Grace is God breaking them.
And if you fall while learning to walk in freedom, do not turn your fall into your identity.
Get up.
Run back to Jesus.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Not casually.
Not presumptuously.
Desperately.
Because sanctification can involve warfare.
Some battles are not over in one emotional altar call.
But the believer does not make peace with the enemy simply because the battle has lasted longer than expected.
You keep fighting.
You keep confessing.
You keep praying.
You keep opening Scripture.
You keep seeking godly community.
You keep returning to the cross.
Not because typing a phrase saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But perhaps somebody else who feels alone needs to discover that there are believers still fighting beside them.
No performance.
No pretending.
Just honesty.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once believed would own you forever, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another wounded person believes freedom is still possible.
That is why this message cannot end with outrage at Corinth.
It must end with hope.
Because Paul rebuked their tolerance of unrepentant sexual immorality, yes.
But he did so in a letter addressed to people who belonged to Christ.
People who needed correction.
People who had been messy.
People whose pasts were anything but spotless.
People Paul could nevertheless describe with three thunderous words:
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
This is Gospel Warrior.
We are not here to help Christians become better stone-throwers.
We are here to keep pointing sinners toward the nail-scarred hands of Jesus Christ.
Before you post it, ask yourself whether your own heart has bowed to the same Word you are asking others to read.
Send it privately to the believer who thinks failure means Jesus is finished with them.
But when believers freely support faithful Gospel work, that support can itself be offered with gratitude to God and used to help truth reach further.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Somebody needs to hear that sin is real.
Somebody needs to hear that judgment is real.
But somebody desperately needs to hear the rest of the Gospel too.
Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
The cross is still enough.
The tomb is still empty.
Grace is still greater than your past.
And Jesus still knows how to turn “such were some of you” into the beginning of a testimony.
So do not merely ask whether Corinth became too tolerant of sin.
Ask the harder question:
Have I become comfortable with anything Jesus died to free me from?
Because the most dangerous chain may not be the one around the person you are judging.
It may be the one you have learned to decorate.
And the most beautiful words waiting on the other side of surrender may still be these:
But you were washed.
But you were sanctified.
But you were justified.
There are scandals the world will remember about you—but when a repentant sinner belongs to Christ, scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
